text: 1552. Bng. sɔmrɛṇɔ ‘to be eager for/after (a fight), to desire’ (with -ɛ- suffix), sɔmrɔ n.m. ‘meeting, gathering (also said about, e.g., the assembling of crows)’ (with -ɔ1 suffix) and sɔmriɔ ‘eagerly’ (with -iɔ suffix); Deog. sɔmrɔ̄ṇɔ ‘to get s.th. ready’. Example Bng.: sɔmriɔ pɔṛɔ zɔgṛe khi eagerly - fallPP.M.S fight.OBL.S for ‘(he) went eagerly to the fight’ < OIA sáṁbhr̥ta- ‘collected’ (12970) (Pa., Pk.). There are derivations in several NIA languages, however a meaning ‘get ready, start’ is, according to Turner, limited to the following Nuristan and Dard languages: Ash., Bashg., Wg. and Kt. To this to be added are Kamd. sāmˈařa ‘set out for; be ready to go; be off to’, Kt. (Strand sub ‘Motion: Object-Relative Motion’) samřé ‘set out for; be ready to go; be off to’ and Brah. sambaring ‘to get ready for a journey’. The meaning of these words seems, however, to be influenced by OIA samará- ‘ hostile encounter, conflict, struggle, war’. In case s.o. wants to recheck the Pahāṛī words, care has to be taken not to confuse this lemma with the almost same sounding sɔmɔrṇɔ̃ ‘to collect, gather, unite’ which is < OIA *saṁvarati ‘restrains’ (13015). Note: there is also Bng. sɔmbeṛṇɔ, sɔ̃beṛṇɔ ‘to collect, gather (e.g., fruits)’ also < OIA 12970. This suggests probably different sub-dialect or borrowing.

text: 1670. Chin. huḍ ‘ewe’ and Paṭṭ. huṛ ‘ram, male sheep’ < OIA eḍa- ‘a kind of sheep’ (2512) (Pa., Pk.) with modern reflexes in the northwest, in S. and Si. Spontaneous aspiration also in Niya Prakrit heḍˈi ‘sheep(?)’ and in Brah. hēṭ ‘she-goat’. But the vowel is unclear. Note that the lemma with initial aspiration has also been borrowed into Psht. heṛə́y ‘sheep with a long tail’ (Cheung [2013: 626, fn. 37]).

text: 16. Bng. kã̄̀ċi ɔ̃ṭhi n.f. ‘small finger’, Khaśdh. kāṇċi ɔ̃̄ṭhi ‘small finger’, Deog. kāṇċi gũ̄ṭhi ‘small finger’, Kṭg. kanċhe ɔṇṭhe ‘the little finger’ (second element in all three cases < OIA aṅguṣṭhá- ‘thumb’ [137]), also Ku. kã̄ś ‘small’ (as in kã̄ś bhɛ̄ ‘little brother’) and N. kã̄ci aũla ‘small finger’ (Z.) — K. of Shrinagar kis, K. of Balmat Kot khʊ̃ch, K. of Banihal khrʌːch, K. of Anantnāg krīs (Sachadeva et al. [2010: 42]) all ‘little fin- ger’, Bhaṭ. qʌčì̄ aṅgùi ‘small finger’, Paš.deg. qčerˈē aṅgoṛek ‘little finger’, Paš. xačˈiː aṅuṛˈeːk ‘little finger’ and dialectal kaṅgučí̄ aṅguṛí̄k ‘little finger’ (first word probably a synonym compound with first syllable < OIA kanya- ‘the smallest’ [2732 ] or *kana- ‘young’), Ḍ. khiˑti aguˑla ‘the little finger’, Sv. kaṇeškuri anguṛí ‘the little finger’ is morphologically unclear but seems also to belong here, Ind. kičìṭʰⁱ ʌṅgùī ‘small fin- ger’ and kʌčɑ̀ʰ ‘small (in size, as a person)’ which is probably same as kʌyčàʰ ‘small; narrow’, and Psht. kačoṭai ‘diminutive, tiny, wee’. Here also with affricatized initial consonant Mult. cīcī ‘little finger or toe’, Brah. čīčak, čīčal, čič-hōr ‘little finger’, Bal. čūč, Jaṭ. cīcī, P. cīcī, S. cīc and Munda Sant. siʔc kəʈuʔ all ‘little finger’; note also Wg. kačkˈi ‘young girl (shortly before sexual maturity)’ and Paš. kučˈuk ‘young- ster’. Cf. also Prs. kūčak ‘little’. The forms, which are cognate with OIA kaniṣṭá- ‘youngest; smallest’ (2718) and kaniṣṭhā- ‘little finger’ (2719) can nevertheless not be derived therefrom, maybe because of contamination with OIA lex. kanyasā- ‘the little finger’. Besides ‘little finger’ and in some cases ‘small penis’ also ‘young girl’ appears to be the main meaning. The latter meaning is also found in an à̄rul song from Ban- gan (Lakshmikant Joshi [2007: 19]), called kedār bāchā ‘The calf of (the mountain tract named) Kedār’ which deals with an episode from the Mahābhārata. There is the following couplet:  tauṁdī kauruvai bhauraṇī pāī, kāṁcchī gaundhārī kauruve biyāhī us samay kauravoṁ ne maṁganī kī, choṭī gāṁdhārī kauravoṁ ko byāhī gaī ‘That time the Kauravas asked for the covenant of a marriage, the young(est) Gāndhārī married the Kauravas’

text: 22. (a) Bng. kuti ‘tickling’ and kutiāṇɔ ‘to tickle’, Jaun. (Z.) kustiyāvṇɔ, Rp. kutkutyai ‘tickling’, N. kutkuti ‘ticklishness’, Rab. kut-kutā- ‘to tickle’, Chit. kitikiti, Deog. kutlaɔṇɔ ‘to tickle s.o.’, Ku. kutkyāi — Bur. qíqit -̇t- and Bur.ys. qétu-qétu both ‘to tickle’, Kho. qéti-qéti, K. kᵃta-kᵃta ‘tickling’, Kamd. katˈakatak ku ‘tickle’, Kal. kitikíti kárik or tikitíki kárik ‘to tickle’ (with karék ‘to tickle someone’), Pr. kiṭə-kiṭək li- ‘to tickle’ and kitəkˈitək ‘tickling’. — B. and Or. kutukutu ‘tickling’, B.roh. kútu ‘feeling funny when touching some parts of the body’ — L. kutkutāṛī, Jaṭ. kutkutāṛī ‘tickling’, S. kutikuti ‘tickling’ and S. kitikitāiṇu ‘to tickle’. (b) Bng. khitkhitāṇɔ ‘to tickle’ — Ind. khít-khitʰ karʌ́v ‘to tickle s.o.’, xìt-xitʰ karʌ́v ‘to tickle (the sole of the foot)’, xʌtì ‘tickling’, xutkulĩ̄ ‘tickle’ (where -kulĩ̄ is related with Pers. kilkil ‘tickling’; also in M.wār. kiċkuli ‘tickling’). (c) Bng. gidgidi ‘tickling’, Khaśdh. gutiauṇɔ ‘to tickle s.o.’ There are also P. gutgutāuṇa ‘to tickle’, M. gudgudī ‘titillation’, Ko.kuṇ. gudguli ‘tickling’, H. gudgudānā ‘to tickle’, B.roh. gudguti ‘backbiting person’, Brah. ɣutlū ‘tickling’ and Deshi Prakrit gilagilāviaṁ (G. galgaliyāṁ) and second member in the near-synonym compound gañjolliaṁ (with first member < OIA *gañj- ‘press, ram’ [3960]) all ‘tickling’ (Bhayani [1988: 71]) — Ora. gutgutū, gutgutī ‘tickling’. I may point out that the PIE root for the very obviously onomatopoeic ‘tickle’ is *geid-, described by Mallory and Adams (2007: 377) as a “Germanic-Armenian isogloss”; however, Watkins suggests the alternative forms of this “expressive root” tit-, tik-, kit- and Lipp quotes Old Nordic kitla and German kitzeln (2009 i: 59), see also Kroonen on Proto-Germanic *kit(t)ōn- ‘to tickle’ (2013: 289). Moreover, many forms compare also with Munda and Mon- Khmer forms, e.g. Bon. kitiʔk- ‘to tickle’, PMK *[k]ti[ ]k ‘to tickle’, Khasi ktik ‘to tickle’, and in case of Deshi Prakrit gilagilāviaṁ and G. galgaliyāṁ one may even think of influence of PIE *gelēi- ‘smile, laugh’, all of which suggests contamination of onomatopoeic forms of different language families.

text: 40. Bng. gùṛi n.f. and Kṭg. and Kc. guṛi all ‘wrinkle’ — K. gĕñi ‘a wrinkle, a crease in the skin or in cloth, etc.’, Ind. ghaṛáṽ and Gau. ghaṛɛ̃̄́ ‘wrinkle’, Bhaṭ. khiri ‘wrin- kle’ — Mult. gundr ‘a fold, a crease in cloth’, P. gann ‘a crease or wrinkle of fat in the abdomen’, S. ɠuñu ‘wrinkle’ wwhich derives according to Turner < OIA guñja² ‘bunch, bundle, cluster’ (4174) where also is listed Kṭg. gunj̈e ‘moustache’ which has a parallel in Bng. gũ̄zɛ n.f.pl. ‘moustache’. It is difficult to reconcile ‘wrinkle’ and ‘moustache’, moreover, there are also related S. ghuñju ‘a pucker, ruffle, rumple, wrinkle’ and New. guji ‘a wrinkle; folds’ which also do not match with 4174 but which match with Psht. gunjaˈh ‘a wrinkle on the face, a furrow, a crease, a crumple, a rum- ple, a pucker, a plait’ and gūnzaˈh ‘a wrinkle, a furrow, a crease’. Note: The relationship of S. ghuñju and Psht. gunjaˈh/gūnzaˈh with Kal. krinǰ ‘wrinkled’ (but Morgenstierne gives Kho. krenǰ and Kal. krīn both ‘wrinkle’ [1936: 659]), Brah. kirinc ‘wrinkle’ and in turn with Pers. kunjulak ‘wrinkle, fold, plait’ and with gurinj ‘a wrinkle’ is not clear. Morgenstierne (ibid.) also refers to Pers. gurinj, Bal. kirišk and Kurd. kurišk all ‘wrinkle’ and suggests for the latter derivation < *kurinčk.
